Published: 03:48 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 07:04 EST, 19 November 2026.

The world has been waiting 13 years for GTA6 and footballers are not immune from the lure and addictive nature of the game.

In fact, top flight players are notorious gamers given their amount of free time after training and Bryan Mbeumo was one of many to share his excitement at the midnight release.

No doubt latest Man United boss Mauricio Pochettino would prefer his players to get a solid night's sleep ahead of taking his first training session on Thursday but Mbeumo couldn't resist a late-night session.

He shared the loading screen of the Rockstar game at midnight on his Instagram story with the word 'historic' as the clock ticked into Thursday morning.

It remains to be seen whether Mbeumo stayed up into the early hours playing but an estimated three million UK adults were expected to call in sick or take annual leave to play.

Sleep is vital for athletes to recover and perform at their best and one NBA star even predicted professionals across sports would see their output 'plummet' as a result of GTA's pull.

Bryan Mbeumo shared this picture on his Instagram story at midnight when GTA went live.

Mauricio Pochettino's first morning of training coincides with the release of GTA, played by Mbeumo and plenty of other athletes who looked forward to the late-night release.

It has been revealed that in a previous video clip online, Mbeumo was being interviewed while on his console and indicated he'd pre-ordered the game, saying: 'I'm just waiting now, the game will make me stay at home every single day... after training.'.

Pochettino, who flew on a private jet to Manchester on Wednesday ahead of his first day in the job on Thursday, will no doubt have a keen eye on whether any of his stars are bleary-eyed in training.

The new boss has an incredibly tight turnaround to prepare for the huge clash with rivals Liverpool on Sunday at Anfield, but perhaps the Reds will also be dealing with GTA-mania.

Alexander Isak was asked about the game's release while on international duty with Sweden and admitted: 'Yeah, so I think it’ll be difficult to reach me from the 19th, when it comes out. I’ll be locked in. That’s the plan.'.

A renowned sleep coach for top athletes, Nick Littlehales, has opined on the effects late-night gaming can have.

'They get lost in it, it’s an engaging distraction, and it satisfies their competitive edge, but just like mindlessly scrolling YouTube or social media, you need to put your own filters and blockers in place, otherwise you’ll find yourself doing something ridiculously stupid and playing for hours and hours, hurting your performance,' he told Ozoon.

According to recent reports, 'We know it’s unrealistic to expect a player to just stop after exactly two hours when they’re in the zone. You have to accept it and ask them: "Are you prepared to sacrifice your nocturnal sleep to be awake and stimulated? Is it worth it?" If they insist on it, we look at scheduling it. Maybe they game late on Tuesdays, Thursdays.

'You must have these open conversations instead of outright banning late-night gaming. If you just throw the book at them, they end up taking sleeping tablets, using snus, and taking unregulated supplements they don’t understand just so they can cope. When you help them manage their gaming, they usually start to self-regulate.'.

Sources indicate that it’s safe to say Bryan Mbeumo is ready for GTA 6. 🤣🤣 pic.twitter.com/skkPM2GYo9.

Conor McGregor announced that he would give employees at various businesses the day off.

People cheer as Grand Theft Auto VI goes live at London gaming venue XP Tavern.

Arsenal's Declan Rice could be another to be locked into the latest GTA having previously spoken about how much gaming helps him switch off.

He told GQ: 'I can never sleep after night games. It’s impossible. I’ll be that wired. I'll play Call of Duty, Grand Theft Auto, FIFA. Anything. Just play with a load of my friends. Adrenaline, everything. You don’t really settle down.

'I feel like when you’re playing at this level, your mind’s just constantly – it’s just going.'.

Football clubs, businesses and even schools are braced for the effects of the newly introduced game, with one head teacher in Chelmsford, Essex, entering students into a raffle to win a £10 Amazon voucher in an attempt to stop them bunking off.

UFC star Conor McGregor announced that he was giving the day off to 400 employees at his various businesses so they could play the game.

And Real Madrid goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois shared an image of himself playing the game, flying a helicopter after it was rolled out.

The astonishing level of anticipation for GTA6 has banked more than £1.14bn in pre-orders alone and is set to become by far the highest grossing game ever made.

It debuted with a score of 99 on review aggregator website Metacritic – equalling 1998's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as the highest-rated video game ever.

Some 2.8million UK adults are set to play the game on launch day alone, according to a Uswitch poll commissioned earlier this month.

Over in the US, a number of athletes were frank in their honesty about how many of them would be addicted to the game.

Real Madrid goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois shared this image from playing the game.

BT and EE called the upcoming launch an 'unprecedented gaming download event' because of the size of the game and the number of people expected to play.

While the exact number of people who have pre-ordered GTA VI is not known, Sony said it is the most pre-ordered game in the history of PlayStation Store.

Sales of gaming consoles and accessories surged in the run-up to launch day.

A man walks past a Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) digital billboard advert in Milan - the game's release has become a global event.

GTA VI returns to the neon-soaked streets of Vice City, Rockstar's fictional version of Miami, which has featured in previous instalments of the series.

The game follows two protagonists, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, who find themselves caught up in a criminal conspiracy in the fictional state of Leonida, inspired by Florida.

The pair become embroiled in a Bonnie and Clyde-style crime story after 'an easy score goes wrong', leaving them 'forced to rely on each other more than ever if they want to make it out alive'.

Breaking: AMD EPYC Zen 6 vs. Zen 1 Performance: 12.1x Geo Mean in Less Than 10 Years

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Phoronix

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This month brought the availability of the latest EPYC 9006 "Venice" SP7 Zen 6 server processors.
  • The AMD EPYC 7601 launched back in June 2017 as the flagship of the EPYC Naples "Zen 1" processors.
  • Now just shy of a decade later, the EPYC 9006 SP7 processors have begun shipping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This month brought the availability of the latest EPYC 9006 "Venice" SP7 Zen 6 server processors. We have seen excellent generational gains with the likes of the EPYC 9686F and EPYC 9996 over Zen 5 Turin CPUs as well as sharply outperforming the competition from Intel and NVIDIA. With the first-generation EPYC "Naples" processors having launched nearly ten years ago, I was curious to quantify AMD's server performance gains over the past decade. So up today is a look at how the EPYC 9996 and EPYC 9686F Zen 6 processors compare to the original EPYC Zen 1 flagship with the EPYC 7601 across real-world workloads for performance as well as power efficiency for some pretty epic gains.

The AMD EPYC 7601 launched back in June 2017 as the flagship of the EPYC Naples "Zen 1" processors. The EPYC 7601 was notable for its time with 32 x Zen 1 cores / 64 threads, 2.2GHz base frequency, 3.2GHz max boost frequency, and 64 MB of L3 cache. On the memory side was eight channel DDR4-2666 memory and for connectivity were up to 128 PCIe 3.0 lanes. The TDP of each EPYC 7601 processor is 180 Watts.

Now just shy of a decade later, the EPYC 9006 SP7 processors have begun shipping. With the AMD EPYC 9996 256-core flagship are 256 Zen 6C cores / 512 threads per socket, 2.55GHz base clock, 4.1GHz max boost frequency, and an incredible 1024MB of L3 cache. EPYC 9006 SP7 processors support DDR5 RDIMMs or up to MRDIMM-12800 memory at 16 channels. There is also 96 lanes of PCI Express 6.0. The EPYC 9996 has a 600W default power rating.

According to recent reports, or for the frequency-optimized flagship is the EPYC 9686F with 96 Zen 5 cores / 192 threads with a 4.05GHz base frequency and up to 5.3GHz maximum boost clock. The EPYC 9686F has a 384MB L3 cache size while also having a 600 Watt default power rating.

Over the past ten years of AMD EPYC there has been incredible architectural advancements too not reflected in the key specs alone such as AVX-512 with Zen 4 and further refined in Zen 5, security improvements to reduce the need for software-based security mitigations, and countless other architectural improvements each step of the way from Zen 1 to Zen 6.

Sources indicate that for comparing EPYC Zen 1 to Zen 6, I dusted off the Dell PowerEdge R7425 server originally provided by AMD for EPYC Naples testing at Phoronix. Nearly ten years later, the Dell PowerEdge server with the dual AMD EPYC 7601 processors still fires up and runs reliably. The AMD EPYC 7601 2P was running with 16 x 32GB DDR4-2666 memory, Samsung SSD 860 SSD storage, and other stock components of this Naples review unit.

With the AMD EPYC 9686F 2P and EPYC 9996 2P testing was the Nigeria reference server with 32 x 64GB MRDIMM-12800 memory, and Micron MTFDMBQ7T6THM-1BP1JABDC PCIe Gen6 SSD.

The AMD EPYC Naples and EPYC Venice servers were tested on the same software stack with using Ubuntu 26.10 for a very up-to-date open-source software experience. Ubuntu 26.10 ships with the Linux 7.3 kernel and GCC 15.3 compiler by default.

In addition to the raw performance testing for EPYC Zen 1 vs. EPYC Zen 6, the CPU power consumption and performance-per-Watt were also compared using the exposed CPU PowerCap/RAPL sensors of 2P processor configuration.

In a recent development, GT Max’s wider field of view provides a more expansive picture, while GT offers a featherweight design. For travel, the appeal is simple: an immaculate 307-inch personal theater that slips right into your daily bag alongside your Apple gear.

Recent findings suggest that the GT Series also functions as an instant, private external display for a USB-C Mac. That makes the glasses invaluable far beyond streaming media, especially when you need an expansive, shoulder-surfer-proof dual-monitor workspace on a flight, train, or co-working desk.

Because the tracking runs on dedicated silicon inside the glasses, none of it taxes the Mac or iPhone you’re plugged into. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I'm an independent security researcher. Over the years I've reported vulnerabilities to a number of vendors and manufacturers, and several of those reports have become CVEs.

Recent findings suggest that for most of the past year I've been working on Google's current Pixel phones. I reverse engineered the Samsung radio stack (under embargo), the IMS and RTP media code, the Trusty trusted apps, the MediaTek M90 modem RIL and the Android telephony framework, amongst other things. In that time I filed 95 reports through the Android and Google Devices Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP), and around 95% of them came with a working proof of concept.

In total, the VRP has paid me $250, in a single payment.

I should say at the outset that I have nothing against Google. My project Box began as a fork of their AI Edge Gallery; I've worked on it most days for a year, and Google have taken features from my fork back into their own. I also maintain Iris, a hardened fork of Chromium. Much of what I do is built on Google's work. This page is solely about what happened to the security bugs I reported through their programme over twelve months.

Industry observers note that bugs were fixed after being closed. For every closed report, I extracted the relevant binary from Google's current factory image and compared the exact function the report referred to. Eight had been fixed in shipped code, with a bounds check, a permission or a validation step added precisely where I'd said one was missing. All eight had originally been closed as a "duplicate" or as "not a vulnerability". None was paid and none was credited. Two more have since been fixed in the QPR3 beta.

Industry observers note that bugs were closed for reasons the code doesn't bear out. More than a dozen others were closed as duplicate, infeasible or "can't reproduce", yet the defect is still there, unchanged, in the current build. I'm not suggesting anyone owes a reward for a bug that hasn't been fixed, and I'm not claiming one. My point is simply that the stated reasons for closing them don't hold up once you look at the binary.

A reward promised in writing has never been paid. In January Google confirmed a valid bug and raised both its severity and its reward, in writing. Three months later they reversed all of it, with no newly introduced evidence. They then noted they would "stand by our word" and pay $250 anyway as a "discretionary payment exception". That was in January. Ten months of "processing", "soon" and "no date" later, it still hasn't been paid. The report itself was submitted before December 2025.

Industry observers note that one line in that thread still puzzles me. Google told me in writing that they were paying the Safety Center reward "even though our final technical assessment rated it as a duplicate of a report with no security impact." If the bug had no security impact, there is nothing to pay for. If it's worth paying for, then it did have an impact. Both statements are in the same ticket.

Sources indicate that everything in the tables below is a closed report, and Google's wording is quoted directly from the problem tracker. I've deliberately left out the technical details of the three reports that are still "Assigned", along with anything under active coordinated disclosure.

Industry observers note that every report on this page is a closed ticket. Google's own position, stated on these tickets, is that they do not grant or deny permission for disclosure and that researchers are free to publish at their discretion. Nothing still under assessment or active coordinated disclosure is included here.

I followed the same process for every closed report in the tables:.

Each report was given one of four verdicts: PATCHED (a check has been added that wasn't there when I reported it), STILL PRESENT (the code is unchanged), N/A (reported against this exact build, or Google described it as intended design) and CANT-DETERMINE (the binary is missing or the build doesn't match).

I didn't rely on Google's security bulletins or the supplementary patch lists. A silent fix with no bulletin entry and no credit won't appear there by definition, so the only way to find one is to compare the shipped code yourself.

Recent findings suggest that this concerns ticket 467575499 / 470814942. On 23 January 2026 Google wrote that they had "confirmed this is a valid bug", were "increasing severity" and "increasing reward", and would "issue a payment for the newly introduced amount once it has been processed". On 24 April, without any further analysis, they reversed all three. In what they called a "Final Assessment", the same bug now "does not qualify for a reward or severity increase".

Industry observers note that in June they wrote that they wished to "stand by our word regarding the reward". On 10 July they set out the figures: "$250 for Safety Center, $250 for the mic bug, $500USD total". They described this as "honoring our initial promise", whilst still referring to the Safety Center half as a duplicate with no security impact. The microphone half was paid. The Safety Center half was moved into a "discretionary payment exception" with, in their words, no "exact credit date". The most recent reply, in October, says much the same: still approved, still no date.

Not every report ended as a duplicate or "not a vulnerability". In this case Google's own panel rated the report High severity, High quality and assigned it for remediation. The fix has since shipped three times: in the QPR3 beta (DP11.261002.005) in October, in the public November stable build (CP4A.261105.040.D1), and in the latest QPR3 beta (DP11.261030.003). The ticket is still marked "Assigned", and the reward and CVE fields are still blank, so I've kept the vulnerability itself out of this write-up. The screenshots below show only the process: a report Google rated High and confirmed in writing as eligible for a reward, then left sitting at "Assigned" after the very condition they had set had been met.

It isn't the only one. A second, unrelated report was also rated High severity, High quality by the same panel. A month later it is still "Assigned", the reward is still "with the panel" and the ASR fields are still blank. I haven't named the report or included any technical detail; the screenshots show only the rating and the state of the reward.

It has been revealed that when Google closes a report as a duplicate, it's closed against an internal "canonical" bug ID. I asked for the IDs behind several of mine. For two entirely unrelated bugs they gave me the same internal ID, 479203197: one was a Rust keystore panic in a trusted app, the other a C++ out-of-bounds read in the RTP media parser. They're written in different languages, sit in different subsystems and belong to different teams. A single internal report cannot be the original for both.

Google acknowledged this in writing on both tickets: "Giving you this ID for your other report was a mistake on our end," and, separately, "we made a mistake when linking the duplicate tickets." So at least one supposedly verified duplicate was marked as such without anyone checking it against the report it named.

Many of my reports followed the same course. Filed, assigned, worked on by an engineer, and then, months later and with no latest technical comment in between, quietly changed to Duplicate. The original is always an internal ticket I can't view, usually accompanied by a note that it was "previously reported by an internal Google engineer". I have no means of seeing that report, confirming that it exists, or confirming that it predates mine.

There are a great many of these. Of the 95 reports I've filed, 34 were closed as duplicates. A few of those are my own resubmissions and appeals folded back together, so it comes to roughly 26 distinct findings that Google accepted as real and then attributed to a report I'm not allowed to see. A duplicate isn't a rejection: it's Google confirming that the bug exists and saying someone else found it first. In 26 of my cases, that someone was an internal engineer who, by Google's account, found the identical bug in the same month I did, in firmware that had only just been released.

It's the timing I keep coming back to. I always work from the current month's factory image, so every report I file concerns firmware released that month, often only a few days earlier. When a bug I found in an image that shipped last week comes back weeks later as something Google has apparently had open internally for months, I'm in no position to check it, and it happens again and again.

On the one occasion I pressed hard enough to find out which build the original was filed against, the explanation was at least plausible. Report 549662989 was marked as a duplicate of one filed against a Pixel 10 (blazer:16/CP1A.260505.005), and PixelModemService ships the same code on both generations, so I accepted it. That was the exception. The ID mix-up described above highlights what the process looks like when I can actually check it: the same internal ID given as the "original" for two completely unrelated bugs, and admitted in writing to be a mistake. If one supposedly verified duplicate was marked without anyone comparing it to the report it named, I've no reason to assume the two dozen I can't check were handled any more carefully.

The DCMO DcmoReceiver bug is a case in point. Google say my re-filed report (585012607) duplicates 545652324, which they describe as having been filed on 12 August 2026 by another external researcher, with the same root cause. I can't confirm any of that. Opening 545652324 returns "Access denied", as has every other original I've been referred to, so the date, the author and the root cause are Google's word alone. What I can check is the code, and the defect is still present and unpatched in CP4A.261105.040.D1, months after the date they give for the original report.

Early on, Google closed one of my findings with their standard message: "not a security vulnerability, logged for potential remediation in a future version, considered closed". They later withdrew it in writing: "You are completely correct. This finding is indeed a legitimate security vulnerability. It was incorrectly closed as 'not a security vulnerability' due to an oversight during triage of this specific ticket.".

The same template has since been used to close several more of my reports. On my own tickets alone it has been shown to be wrong more than once, by Google's own admission, and the concern was subsequently patched using the code I had submitted.

In a recent development, from now on, whenever Google closes one of my reports, I'll publish it here. The two reports below were closed in the same way, so it's worth being precise about what happened. Both had already been assigned and triaged. A Google triager then manually moved each one back to "Latest", and a minute later, from the same personal account, posted a message describing itself as "an automatically generated message" from the "Google Security Bot". The message closed the report as Won't Fix (Intended Behavior) on the grounds of a rate limit, and stated "we will not be able to see any of your responses".

The genuinely automated messages on my tickets come from a separate system account. These came from the person who had handled the ticket manually a minute before, which is difficult to reconcile with an automated rate limiter. The second report was closed in this way even after I'd supplied a full reproduction on a locked, release-keys phone. Both defects can be verified directly from the shipping image.

This is ticket 559521028. The MediaTek RIL on the Pixel 11 (libmtkmipc-ril.so, loaded by mtkfusionrild) reimplements the AOSP SMS, WAP push and 3GPP2 parsers in native C++, but keeps AOSP's habit of indexing buf[i] without checking bounds. In Java, reading past the end of a buffer throws an exception that gets caught. In native code nothing is thrown, so an over-read leaks memory and an over-write corrupts it.

There are two defects. Both can be reached with a single incoming SMS, with no user interaction and no app installed:.

Use the leak to defeat ASLR, then use the write to corrupt a chosen object. That's the standard route to remote code execution in rild, the radio daemon, which runs as the radio user and has a direct channel to the baseband.

It has been revealed that I was particularly specific about how the code is reached. The RIL does have one sanity check on PDUs, smsDeliverPduCheck, but it only sits on the branch that forwards the raw PDU to the framework. The native parser is reached by a separate path, from dispatchSms to onHandleSmsMessage to dispatchSuplMsg to SmsMessage::createFromPdu, with no check on it at all. That path depends on a SUPL gate, doesSuplExist(), which returns true for as long as rild is running on any normal device: its global is initialised to 2 in .data (confirmed in the shipped binary) and changes to 1 as soon as MediaTek's location daemon starts. The unchecked parser therefore runs on every incoming SMS, and the trigger can be a silent Type 0 SMS that the user never sees.

In a recent development, I re-checked both defects in three shipped builds: the October stable release (CD1A.261005.003), the November stable release (CP4A.261105.040.D1, SPL 2026-11-05) and the DP11 QPR3 beta. No bounds check had been added to any of these paths.

This is static analysis of the shipped binary. I don't have a modem test rig, as the report makes clear, so there's no runtime exploit attached. On 12 November the team asked for a live software proof of concept. Two days later, on 14 November, the report was closed as Won't Fix (Infeasible) with the template "we have investigated this glitch and determined that this is not a security vulnerability... logged for potential remediation in a future version", and the ASR Severity field was set to NSBC. That is the same template Google have already withdrawn on another of my reports, here applied to an unchecked, attacker-controlled memcpy length in the radio daemon that can be reached with zero clicks and is still present in the shipping build.

A few more of the closed reports, kept short. Each is the bug, roughly how it works, and how it is reached.

An OTA update the device will install, signed by the wrong key (ticket 541986810, closed Duplicate). RecoverySystem.verifyPackage is the check that decides whether an update package is really signed by Google. It looks at two certificates and never confirms they are the same one. The trust check looks at the certificate sitting first in the package. The signature is then verified against a different certificate, chosen by an issuer and serial number that are also read from the package. So an attacker puts Google's genuine, public signing certificate first to pass the trust check, puts their own certificate further in, points the signature at that one, and signs the package with their own key. The check passes for a package they signed. It is reached through the sideload or update path, where the signature gate that is supposed to stop an unofficial package does not.

In a recent development, DNS still leaves the phone when you turn on "Block connections without VPN" (ticket 552188030, closed Duplicate). VPN lockdown is meant to stop any traffic that is not inside the tunnel. DNS queries are left exempt from that block, for every app, not just the device's own traffic. So even with lockdown on, an app's DNS lookups leave the device outside the VPN, which leaks which sites are being resolved and gives a channel the lockdown is supposed to close.

In a recent development, any app can switch off your Lock-on-Disconnect (ticket 552305734, closed Infeasible, still present). The Cross-Device stack exports a broadcast receiver, PermissionBroadcastReceiver, with no permission on it, and it acts on the broadcast without checking who sent it. Any installed app, holding no permissions, can send that broadcast and force an immediate un-enrollment of the user's Lock-on-Disconnect security feature, turning off a protection the user had switched on.

The share sheet fetching a picture it should not (ticket 538314136, closed Infeasible, still present). The intent resolver renders a caller-supplied icon URI without checking the caller is allowed to read it. An app hands it a URI that points at content belonging to another user or profile, and a privileged process fetches it on the attacker's behalf and hands it back.

Any app cancelling another app's on-device AI model load (ticket 558472707, closed Infeasible, still present). cancelModelLoad in the NPU manager service does not check who is calling, so any app can cancel a different app's model load and deny it the hardware AI path.

Sources indicate that A radio service you can crash with one value (ticket 555984702, closed Can't Reproduce, still present). The grilservice radio-config path reads an array size straight from an incoming parcel with no cap and allocates it. A crafted size forces a huge allocation and takes the service down, dropping telephony.

Recent findings suggest that any app can bind the Play Store's setup service (ticket 564059393, closed Working As Intended). Play Store exports IPlaySetupServiceV2, and the permission meant to guard it declares no protection level, so Android treats it as a normal permission and auto-grants it to any app that asks. Any installed app can then bind the service. The same pattern, a guard permission with no protection level so it auto-grants, turned up across 31 exported components in the shipped image.

An unprotected "setup finished" broadcast that rewrites your system locale (ticket 563958561, closed Infeasible). SETUP_WIZARD_FINISHED is not a protected broadcast, so any app can send it. Nine privileged, system-UID receivers act on it, and one of them persistently rewrites the device's system locale. A zero-permission app sends one broadcast and changes a system-wide setting it has no right to touch.

Recent findings suggest that A preinstalled app slipping past the account-ownership check (ticket 559524832, closed Infeasible). AccountManagerService.isSystemUid() actually tests whether the caller is preinstalled, not whether it is the system UID. Any preinstalled app therefore passes a guard meant only for the system, and can see and remove accounts it does not own.

Recent findings suggest that faking that you are standing next to your car (ticket 560453159, closed Can't Reproduce). Two chained UWB bugs: one leaks the secure-ranging session key, the other hijacks the Digital Key radio path. Together a zero-permission app could spoof the physical proximity that passive car entry relies on, without being anywhere near the vehicle.

Recent findings suggest that one Wi-Fi frame reading out of bounds in the kernel (ticket 568933934, closed Can't Reproduce). An unsigned integer underflow in the Broadcom Wi-Fi driver's QoS-Map action-frame handler causes an out-of-bounds read in kernel heap memory. A single 25-byte 802.11 action frame from a nearby Wi-Fi peer triggers it, with no association or pairing.

According to recent reports, A VoLTE call message that hangs the IMS stack (ticket 560878423, closed Can't Reproduce). A SIP message with a negative Content-Length is parsed as a signed value, the offset goes negative, and the receive loop never ends. One zero-click message puts the VoLTE/IMS stack into a permanent hang.

Sources indicate that any app reading and tampering with your Now Playing history (ticket 562215877, closed Infeasible). Private Compute Services exports NowPlayingRelayService as a binder with no caller check, unlike four sibling services in the same app. Any installed app can read and alter the record of music the phone has recognised around you.

In a recent development, any app triggering a recognition pass and reading the result (ticket 561838690, closed Infeasible). The Android System Intelligence MusicRelayService binder does no caller check across its 19 transactions, so any app can read your Now Playing history and silently start a latest recognition pass, listening to what is around you.

An RCS suggestion that runs JavaScript in-app with one tap (ticket 572199671, closed Working As Intended). Google Messages' blocklist for RCS suggested-action URLs misses the javascript: and data: schemes, so a crafted suggestion loads into a JavaScript-enabled bridged WebView, and one tap runs the attacker's JavaScript inside the app.

Industry observers note that any app reading the CBRS radio database and its coordinates (ticket 579289116, closed Duplicate). The CbsdContentProvider in SCONE is exported with no guard, so any installed app can read the CBRS CBSD database, including the CBSD location coordinates, that it should have no access to.

A Wi-Fi attribute reading out of bounds in the kernel (ticket 547477982, closed Duplicate). The Broadcom Wi-Fi driver does not validate a NAN SDEA attribute length before using it, so a crafted value causes an out-of-bounds read in kernel memory. It is reachable from a nearby Wi-Fi peer.

In a recent development, A system service handed the keys to start anything (ticket 558470054, closed Infeasible). dcservice, an app-tier component, is given the SELinux permission to start any init service, the only domain on the whole device with that broad grant, and for a capability its own code never uses. It is exactly the kind of over-grant that turns a small foothold into a larger one.

It has been revealed that the SDK sandbox taking attacker file paths (ticket 561840524, closed Can't Reproduce). computeSdkStorage is the one method on the SDK Runtime sandbox service that is missing the check that the caller is the system server, so any zero-permission app can bind the service and call it with paths of its choosing.

Recent findings suggest that A two-byte location message that exhausts the stack (ticket 568936058, closed Can't Reproduce). The GNSS daemon's SUPL message framing recurses into itself with no base case when a message declares a zero length, so a two-byte message drives it into infinite recursion and crashes the daemon.

It has been revealed that A WAP-push SMS that quietly kills texting (ticket 543183960, closed Infeasible). A malformed WAP-push message lands in a loop with an empty catch block, so instead of failing cleanly the telephony process hangs and SMS silently stops working.

It has been revealed that A SIP message body that overflows a stack buffer (ticket 540746953, closed Duplicate). The IMS SIP encoder copies a message body into a fixed 65535-byte array on the stack with no cap, so an oversized body overflows it.

An eUICC revision any app can kick off (ticket 532021672, closed Infeasible). StartOtaReceiver is exported and unprotected, so any unprivileged app can trigger the eUICC OTA flow by sending the broadcast it listens for.

A system app that fetches URLs for you (ticket 537921665, closed Working As Intended). ConfigUpdater's exported receivers take a URL from broadcast extras and fetch it, with no checks, so an app with no INTERNET permission can make a system app perform requests on its behalf, a server-side request forgery.

Tethered traffic walking straight past VPN lockdown (ticket 552196751, closed Infeasible). "Block connections without VPN" does not cover tethered clients, so anything connected over USB, Ethernet or the Wi-Fi hotspot bypasses the VPN entirely. Google closed it as working by construction.

It has been revealed that any app repainting the real enterprise-enrollment screen (ticket 552200665, closed Infeasible). A zero-permission app can drive the phone's genuine enterprise-enrollment screen and place its own logo on it, on demand, which is the groundwork for a convincing enrollment phish.

Impersonating another process by renaming yourself (ticket 559533853, closed Infeasible). The process-monitor daemon identifies the process it watches only by reading /proc/pid/cmdline, with no UID check when the vendor config leaves the uid out. Any app can set its own process name to match the target and be treated as it.

An NFC firmware-update reply read past its buffer (ticket 537923579, closed Duplicate). The NFC firmware-update handler indexes into the response from the NFC chip using a length it does not check. It sits on the trust boundary with the physically attached NFC controller.

Any app making a system installer install an APK (ticket 563677600, closed Duplicate). WebAppService runs as a privileged app holding INSTALL_PACKAGES. By declaring a single intent-filter, any zero-permission app can make it install an APK, borrowing its install privilege.

A CDMA text message that overflows the radio daemon's stack (ticket 568929629, closed Duplicate). The MediaTek RIL's CDMA CT-WAP SMS decoder (BearerData::specialProcessForCtWapPush) writes past a fixed buffer on a crafted message, with no interaction. This is the write half of the SMS chain described above, filed on its own.

In a recent development, A reported heap write in the Messages image decoder (ticket 537918512, closed Working As Intended). A crafted animated-WebP image delivered by MMS or RCS, where the frame-disposal step in libframesequence was reported to clear a region using a width and height taken from the file without clamping them, overflowing the pixel buffer. Google closed it Working As Intended, and unlike most of the entries here I could not fully confirm the path in the shipped binary, so it is listed as reported and closed rather than verified.

Each row is a closed report, checked against Google's current factory image. "Fixed" means the code the report described has changed: the report was right, the fix shipped, the ticket stayed closed and nothing was paid.

That's eight tickets, closed as duplicate or infeasible, that have been fixed in the shipping image. I re-checked all eight against the October builds and the fixes are still in place.

Two more have been fixed in the QPR3 beta (DP11.261002.005) but not yet in a stable release:.

On 30 October 2026 another researcher independently disclosed a zero-click WAP push crash in Android's telephony stack (smsofdeath.com), which has been reported here: cybersecuritynews.com/zero-click-android-vulnerability. A single malformed WAP push SMS causes WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu to allocate an array from an unvalidated, truncated header length. This throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException that kills the telephony process, and because the carrier keeps redelivering the unacknowledged message, one SMS becomes a recurring outage.

I reported that exact defect twice, with the root cause in WspTypeDecoder and WapPushOverSms traced frame by frame, and a working proof against the shipped decoder:.

In a recent development, both were closed as duplicates of internal report 517376969, which Google say was filed by their internal automated testing in late May 2026. The fix, a bounds check before the allocation, shipped in the QPR3 beta (DP11.261002.005) and is still missing from the current stable build. On 30 October 2026 Google told me on the record that, because their internal tool found it first, my reports are "not eligible for a reward".

So in this one pair of tickets you can see the whole pattern: reported early, verified against the source, closed as a duplicate, fixed without comment in a later build, disclosed publicly by someone else, and never paid.

Recent findings suggest that the clearest way to see this is to put two factory images with the same patch level side by side. Take the WAP push crash (538367541 / 543174762, closed as Duplicate) and the SIM Toolkit crash (555981160, closed as "not reproducible" and later changed to Duplicate). Both are closed, and neither was paid.

The same file, at the same security patch level, in two builds:.

The bug was real enough to fix, and the fix is in a shipping build. Yet the report that found it, and described that exact fix, was closed as a duplicate or a non-problem and paid nothing. The credit went instead to an internal report I'm not allowed to see, filed on a date I can't verify, against firmware that had only just been released.

I'm not claiming payment for any of these; none of them has been fixed. They're listed because the reason given for closing each one doesn't match the code. The defect is still there, unchanged, in the current factory image. Every one of these reports has been closed.

Other researchers have described much the same experience with Google's reward programmes. These are the cases that have been reported publicly.

In a recent development, config Connector, 2026. In June 2026 The Register reported on Justin O'Leary's "ConfigConfusion" flaw in Google Config Connector, which allowed a user in one Kubernetes namespace to obtain organisation owner rights in GCP. He reported it on 8 March. Google replied "Nice catch!", rated it P1/S1 and accepted it, then reversed its position, said the product was working as intended and refused the reward. Google's view was that not paying a reward "does not mean that the product team won't fix the glitch". Months later the ticket still showed as accepted, with no CVE and no fix. O'Leary's argument was straightforward: if it needs fixing, it isn't intended behaviour, and if it isn't intended behaviour, it qualifies for a reward.

Antigravity, 2025. When Google rolled out its Antigravity AI coding tool, researchers at Mindgard reported that a tampered workspace could plant code that would run every time the application started. Google closed the report on 21 November as "Won't Fix (Intended Behavior)", and only reopened and escalated it after Mindgard published their findings four days later. The matter was later fixed.

Industry observers note that pixel lock screen bypass, 2022. David Schütz found that he could unlock a Pixel without its passcode by swapping the SIM card and entering the PUK code. He reported it in June 2022 and, some months later, was told it was a duplicate. The earlier report was one Google had been unable to reproduce. Only after he kept pressing, and demonstrated the bypass to Google engineers in person, was it fixed in the November 2022 enhancement (CVE-2022-20465). He was paid $70,000, rather than the $100,000 available for a lock screen bypass, because his report was still treated as a duplicate.

In a recent development, in 2020 CSO Online covered the wider problem (J.M. Porup, "Bug bounty platforms buy researcher silence, violate labor laws, critics say"). Critics in that piece, including legal scholars such as Amit Elazari and Katie Moussouris, argue that these programmes can be used to suppress disclosure, that researchers often have no legal safe harbour, and that the model raises questions under labour law. The description of researchers as disposable contractors whose finished work can be rejected without recourse is mine, not theirs.

How to Make a Lovable City

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3260 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Worksinprogress

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, everyone loves the streets of old cities like Verona, Bruges, and Prague.
  • The Austrian architect Camillo Sitte (pronounced ‘zitter’) sought to explain what makes some public spaces more successful than others in a lively, opinionated masterpiece called The Art of Building Cities, published in 1889.
  • In a recent development, sitte’s book was explosively successful, seizing the imagination of late nineteenth-century Europe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, everyone loves the streets of old cities like Verona, Bruges, and Prague. The reason might seem obvious: they are lined by beautiful historic buildings. But people also love the streets of Osaka, Taipei, and Hong Kong. While the buildings of the latter cities are mostly modern and nondescript, their streets are still full of character and enchantment.

The Austrian architect Camillo Sitte (pronounced ‘zitter’) sought to explain what makes some public spaces more successful than others in a lively, opinionated masterpiece called The Art of Building Cities, published in 1889. Sitte argued that the best public spaces are physically enclosed and fairly small, creating a sense of shelter and intimacy, defining picturesque views and perspectives, and making public buildings appear larger and more dignified by comparison. He denied the importance of symmetry and claimed, counterintuitively, that monuments should be pushed to the edge of squares, and that great public buildings should generally be entangled in a mass of everyday housing.

In a recent development, sitte’s book was explosively successful, seizing the imagination of late nineteenth-century Europe. For a few decades, Sitte was a decisive figure in international urban planning, and planners across the world strove to implement his ideas. But after modernism came to dominate Western planning in the mid-twentieth century, Sitte was mostly forgotten.

Recent findings suggest that sitte’s attacks were directed against the repetitive grids, sweeping boulevards, and impersonal regularity of most nineteenth-century urban planning. To many people today, however, nineteenth-century urbanism is relatively appealing; certainly, it is a lot more attractive than the motorways, slab blocks, and concrete plazas that came after. This can make Sitte strange to read, but it also makes him even more important now than he was in his own time.

It has been revealed that anyone who wants to build beautiful cities today needs to understand what it is that makes the most beloved cities of the past so successful. Focusing only on the appearance of buildings can only get you so far. As Sitte highlighted, some of the world’s most impressive buildings are badly let down by their surroundings, and form part of inhospitable and uninviting public spaces. Equally, neighborhoods consistent with Sittean principles can be wonderfully charming even if their constituent buildings are nothing special. Understanding these principles may be the key to building new neighbourhoods and cities that people truly love being in.

The first principle of The Art of Building Cities is the importance of creating physically enclosed public spaces. People feel calmer and more protected in such spaces, which they experience as ‘outdoor rooms’. An enclosed outdoor area can also develop its own character, just as kitchens, bedrooms, and bathrooms have their respective characters. Sitte would have seen a city without enclosed public spaces as analogous to an extremist open-plan house, where the kitchen, bedroom and bathroom are open onto each other and bleed constantly into one another’s character.

Industry observers note that while the rooms of a house are created with partition walls, the enclosed spaces of a city are created with buildings. A conundrum for urban designers is that the building wall of a square generally has to be repeatedly broken to provide access. A square is thus like a room with five or ten large doors, permanently left wide open, undermining its sense of enclosure. Sitte was keenly interested in how to handle the entrances to squares so as to mitigate this.

According to recent reports, the picture above highlights the Grand-Place of Brussels. Most of the entrances are at the corners, and at each corner, only one street enters. These streets continue the plane of the square rather than entering at a diagonal. This means that, from almost any point in the square, the two building walls appear to overlap each other, effectively concealing the entrance to the street and preserving the sense of enclosure. The resulting ‘turbine square’ is so common in old towns that, as Sitte said, ‘it can be considered as one of the conscious or subconscious principles of ancient city building’.

Even better than a turbine square, in Sitte’s view, was one whose entrances had been bridged over, creating a fully continuous building line around the square. This is particularly common in Spain. The Plaça Reial in Barcelona has seven entrances, but six have been bridged over, so that the square feels like a courtyard or cloister. Colonnades, which Sitte thought to be a greatly underrated device in urban design, provide a simple way to achieve this.

In a recent development, london’s Trafalgar Square is an example of the opposite, a ‘square’ that is only weakly enclosed. Wherever one stands, one can generally see two or more of the wide and busy roads that join it. Like many nineteenth-century squares, Trafalgar Square was never intended to be an enclosed space, but rather was designed to improve the flow of carriages between the Strand and the West End.

An even more extreme example of an unenclosed ‘square’ is the Place de la Concorde in Paris, which has no fewer than nine roads entering and exiting it, and buildings on only one side. The space is bewildering and demoralizing for pedestrians, who must work their way across successive roads without buildings to shape their route and shelter them on their way.

Sitte applied this logic to streets as well as squares, arguing that curves and T-junctions should be used to visually terminate streets and give them a sense of enclosure. The picture above reveals Broad Street, one of America’s rare curving streets. The combination of the curve of the street and partial T-junction at the end means that Broad Street is visually closed by the Federal Hall National Memorial, creating a famously beautiful and charismatic space. The second photograph shows a more typical Manhattan street, experienced as an endless canyon separating continents of buildings, what Sitte called ‘parallels vanishing at infinity’.

In a recent development, if a square is too large, it loses its sense of enclosure, and its buildings look strangely diminished by their surroundings. Sitte provided a rule of thumb in sizing squares: the dimensions of a square should not be greater than twice the height of the principal building in it. The pictures above show two examples of over-large squares: the Plaza de la Armería in Madrid and Heroes’ Square in Budapest. Both feel demoralizingly vast, with the monumental buildings they are meant to showcase (Madrid Cathedral, and Budapest’s Hall of Art) dwindling to visual insignificance on the horizon, so that they resemble doll’s houses. In both squares, the buildings are so miniaturized that they no longer seem like enclosing walls, leaving the visitor exposed in a huge open space. This problem could be solved by making the buildings much taller, but although the square would then feel enclosed, the buildings would have become terrifyingly huge, as if meant for giants rather than human beings (the courtyard of Les Espaces d’Abraxas near Paris is an example of this pitfall in the wild).

Sources indicate that some of the world’s most famous squares are, in fact, far too large. St Peter’s Square in the Vatican, seen above, was designed by the famous artist Bernini, and it does indeed look impressive in drone footage. For human visitors, however, it is an exhausting place, overwhelming without being impressive. The Basilica looks small and stubby, exactly the opposite of the desired effect. On a summer’s day, the vast, unshaded space becomes relentlessly inhospitable, and visitors huddle under the colonnades for shelter.

By contrast, the small square in front of the Pantheon in Rome exemplifies the features Sitte prized. It is impossible to fully capture its feeling of enclosure in a two-dimensional photograph, but some sense of the intimacy of the space is apparent in the pictures above, which show how this magnifies the Pantheon. The Pantheon is a smaller building than Madrid Cathedral or Saint Peter’s Basilica, but it is much bigger relative to the square. This allows it to retain its dignity, despite the fact that the level of the street has risen by 1.3 meters since Antiquity, swallowing the steps that originally led up to the entrance.

At the time Sitte was writing, many planners believed that harmonious spaces should have regular, symmetrical intends, an idea which remains influential today. In English we even use the confusing word ‘square’ for any enclosed public spaces, whatever their shape.

Industry observers note that sitte rejected this, believing that symmetrical spaces do not necessarily feel harmonious at ground level, and that asymmetry is not generally disharmonious at all. The pictures above show the perfectly symmetrical Place Vendôme in Paris. Seen from a satellite, it is visually striking and certainly neater than an irregular space. Its chamfered initiative supposedly inspired the design of Chanel’s No 5 perfume bottle. Pedestrians, however, generally do not stand at the exact point at which the objective balance of the buildings is reflected in their field of vision: the various points and angles from which they do experience it may even make it feel quite awkward.

Above is the Piazza delle Erbe, a market square in Verona. This ‘square’ has an odd shape, an elongated and slightly wonky pentagon. Nobody is likely to model perfume bottles on it. But at human level, this does not matter as pedestrians can never take in all five sides at once, and so its irregular form is barely even visible. For the most part, the irregularities are ‘seen only on paper’, and to the extent they are visible, they are not experienced as imperfections. Sitte argued that they in fact serve to subtly arouse visual interest, and also create happy recesses that can host resting places, statues, or other public art.

According to recent reports, if you were putting an ornament in your living room, you would be very unlikely to stand it in the middle of the carpet. It would get in the way, break up the space, and might well look lost and isolated. Nor would you place it in front of one of the room’s main features, like the fireplace. It would block the view of the fireplace, and the fireplace would be a disagreeably busy backdrop. Almost certainly, you would put it against the wall, preferably a relatively neutral wall to create a calm background.

Industry observers note that sitte thought the same considerations applied to the placing of sculptures, fountains, and other monuments in outdoor spaces. Statues should not be placed in the middle of squares, where they would block natural routes, break up the space, and look isolated and diminished. Nor should they be placed on axes with key buildings, where they block the view of the architecture. Instead they should line the sides, where they can stand out against relatively neutral backgrounds.

In a recent development, this was implicitly understood in Antiquity, the Middle Ages, and the Renaissance, and Sitte illustrates his book with examples from all three periods. Above, for example, is the Piazza della Signoria in Florence. The numerous statues line the sides of the square, leaving the center free for people to pass through or mill about. This is advantageous for the statues too: Michelangelo’s David (today a replica, since the original was moved indoors) stands out splendidly against the plain masonry walls of the Palazzo Vecchio.

Recent findings suggest that later planners became fascinated by the apparent neatness of centering statues. Above is the Victoria Memorial in London. The Memorial stands on the main axis of the Mall, blocking the view of Buckingham Palace behind it. This is not advantageous for the Memorial either, whose outline clashes confusedly with the complex detailing of the building. If you search through pictures of the Memorial, you will notice that most photographers picture it from an awkward oblique angle, the least bad way to capture both the monument and the central pavilion of the palace.

Industry observers note that isolating statues against the sky is not much better. A bronze cast of David was later placed on the Piazzale Michelangelo, at the center of a wide square with stunning views over Florence. The statue is enormous, over five meters tall, but it looks strangely miniaturized in its location. Sitte remarked that contemporary tourists often came away with the drastically false impression that it was life-sized. We judge size partly by comparison, and when an object is isolated from comparators, its size becomes harder to assess. This is why the backdrop of a wall can make sculpture look bigger and grander by providing a constant visual key.

In Sitte’s view, the plain edge of a small square was not only an acceptable site for a statue, but the best one. Sitte disliked museums, which he called ‘art prisons’, and thought that only people with a ‘special mental preparation’ could enjoy art under their ‘morbid influences’. The Sittesque city would be one that teemed with art, but woven into the urban fabric as an adornment of ordinary civic life.

In a recent development, sitte’s view on buildings was similar. Nineteenth-century architects tended to place major public buildings in the middle of squares, judging that this gave them greater dignity. Sitte thought this ‘pedantic, futile modern practice’ destroyed the square and squandered the opportunity to frame the public building with vernacular architecture. He pointed out that many historic cities were in fact designed along the lines he proposed. Of the 255 churches of Rome, 41 adjoined other buildings on one side, 96 on two, 110 on three, and two on all four. Only six were freestanding, two of them modern churches of expatriate Protestant communities.

The most striking examples of this arose when nineteenth-century governments actually demolished the vernacular buildings that surrounded historic monuments. This practice, often known by its French name dégagement, was surprisingly common: nineteenth-century planners thought that it displayed the monuments better. It provides a useful experiment on the effect of freestanding versus adjoined monumental architecture.

In a recent development, for example, Notre Dame Cathedral was formerly approached through a narrow street called the Rue Neuve Notre Dame. The street was demolished by the government planner Haussmann in the nineteenth century to create the Parvis Notre-Dame, a large square that the cathedral still faces today. Haussmann intended to improve the view of the cathedral, but the effect is the opposite. The vernacular fabric formed a visual frame, defining and concentrating views onto the facade. It provided scale, making the cathedral look larger by contrast to the ordinary buildings around it. It also prevented visitors from seeing the whole facade until they were very close, close enough that it towered up terrifically before them. Exposed and isolated, Notre Dame looks smaller and lonelier.

Sitte thought that cities should move in the opposite direction. The Votive Church in Vienna was built in the 1870s on what Sitte described as a ‘desolate monster plaza’ that was ‘intolerably exposed to high wind, inclement weather, heat and dust, as well as to the din of the streets, and the incessant clanging of trams.’ The church does indeed have an awkward and lonely feeling. Sitte thought that the architecture of the building was actually very good, and that the defects in its effect were entirely the fault of its location. He proposed building up regular urban fabric on most of the ‘monster plaza’, defining three small squares with well-framed views onto the church. Sitte’s motives were aesthetic, but we should also note the density and spatial efficiency of his scheme.

Another way to understand this contrast is to look at whole cities planned on Sittesque and anti-Sittesque principles. The pictures below show Padua and Washington DC. It is as though a figure-ground switch has taken place: in Padua, the buildings are molded around spaces; in Washington, space is molded around buildings. Monumental buildings in Washington sit alone on their city blocks, untouched by vernacular fabric. Monumental buildings in Padua constantly link up with vernacular fabric to shape small, sheltered spaces from which they can be properly enjoyed.

According to recent reports, the Art of Building Cities was an immediate success, landing, in the words of Sitte’s English translator Charles T Stewart, ‘like a demolition bomb on the city planning practices of Europe’. Within a year of publication it had prompted the redrawing of urban expansion plans in Germany and Austria, and Sitte was being approached by town officials seeking his advice on their own plans. By Sitte’s death in 1903, advocates of his ideas were to be found in prestigious positions in cities including Munich, Berlin, and Vienna, either teaching or as official city architects.

Recent findings suggest that two Helsinki neighborhoods demonstrate the effect of Sittesque ideas on urban planning. In the nineteenth century, Helsinki followed a neoclassical grid proposal, with straight streets meeting at right angles. In the early twentieth century, it switched dramatically to a Sittesque approach, introducing curving streets, turbine squares, T-junctions, and asymmetrical spaces. The resulting neighborhood is full of pleasing, characterful spaces and unexpected ‘old town’ effects, even though it is made up of the same tall apartment buildings and wide streets as its predecessor.

Recent findings suggest that but Sitte’s influence was curiously short-lived. In the decades following Sitte’s death in 1903, European urban design came to be dominated by the modernist movement. Everything that Sitte hated about nineteenth-century planning was vastly amplified in modernism. With honorable exception, the modernists treated public space as merely whatever was left over after the buildings had been placed, and had no sympathy with Sitte’s approach of treating spaces as primary and shaping the buildings around them. Instead of lining the edge of a city block with buildings (a ‘perimeter block’) they preferred to orient all blocks in the same direction (‘parallel blocks’), often with a seemingly arbitrary angle to the street. Sitte had decried the gridiron blocks of the nineteenth century for the weakly defined spaces they created. But by twentieth-century standards, the straight ‘corridor streets’ of the nineteenth century look comparatively Sittesque.

Modernists also wanted to reduce the built footprint, leaving more space for greenery, parking, and roads. Sitte’s preference for small squares and enclosed spaces was in tension with this. Many modernists saw him as an impractical romantic. The critic Sigfried Giedion described Sitte as ‘a kind of troubadour, ineffectually pitting his medieval songs against the din of modern industry’.

Ironically, modernism proved to be Sitte’s great vindication, as modernist planning has been repudiated almost worldwide. Architects of all stylistic persuasions have once again become interested in streets and squares, in creating public spaces with intimacy and character. Designers associated with the ‘Newly introduced Urbanist’ movement are often openly followers of Sitte, and famous New Urbanist towns like Seaside in Florida, I’On in South Carolina, and Poundbury in Dorset were explicitly designed under Sitte’s influence. But the Sittesque revival goes far beyond this. Prominent contemporary practices like Ash Sakula and Peter Barber produce highly Sittesque urban designs, creating intimate infill schemes that recall the old towns and bazaar districts of the Middle Ages.

Mainstream development is moving in the same direction, but slowly and often incompetently. Many recent attempts to make traditional streets and squares look awkward or stilted. This should not surprise us: building cities is an art perfected over hundreds of years. City-builders today are lucky that Sitte distilled and recorded its key principles, just before the art itself was lost. Studying Sitte can help us to relearn it.

Phoebe Arslanagic-Little is a writer and policy researcher.Samuel Hughes is an editor at Works in Progress.

This season, Rice has been challenged to impact play more in the final third. 💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I think Apple can reasonably claim to be the leading tech giant when it comes to its environmental credentials. It has led the way with its use of renewable energy, made significant strides with carbon-neutral production, and removed plastic from all its packaging.

All of this could potentially be put at risk by the company’s ambitions for Siri AI, however, as Meta joins Google in admitting it is now unlikely to meet its own 2030 net zero promise, thanks to the huge power demands of the data centers powering its AI services ….

According to recent reports, apple’s environmental record isn’t entirely perfect. For example, when it claimed that the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2 were carbon neutral back in 2023, that claim was described as “bogus,” with the EU banning Apple from repeating it. The firm has also been criticized for pushing a relentless annual iPhone cycle, encouraging frequent upgrades.

In a recent development, overall, however, Apple has first-rate credentials when it comes to the environment. It was way back in 2018 when the firm hit its goal of running its own operations off 100% renewable energy. This includes all Apple facilities, from Apple Park through data centers to its worldwide retail store network.

I noted at the time that using more environmentally friendly packaging should be the company’s next priority, and it has indeed made great progress with this over the years, succeeding in removing all plastic packaging earlier this year.

According to recent reports, after its own operations, Apple set about trying to tackle the power usage of its manufacturing partners. Back in 2020, the firm set a goal of having its entire supply chain be carbon neutral by 2030. Just four years later, Apple stated it was 95% of the way there.

It has been revealed that the company also helps fund and support a wide range of environmental initiatives around the world. Just a few examples include conservation in China’s national parks, environmental protection and carbon removal in Australia and Latest Zealand, and helping to fund the build-out of renewable energy capacity in India.

According to recent reports, potentially, however, the vast energy demands of the data centers powering AI services could put its 2030 goal at risk. Other tech giants have already admitted that it may lead them to fail to hit their own renewable energy promises.

Sources indicate that back in 2024, for example, Google CEO Sundar Pichai said that the AI boom was “challenging” to the company’s 2030 carbon-free goal. CNET reports that Meta is now also admitting that it may fail to hit the same target.

Meta’s data center and sustainability chiefs wrote that the organization is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones — including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets.” In an emailed statement to CNET, a Meta spokesperson added, “We remain committed to net zero, but are re-evaluating the 2030 timeline.”.

Notably, a lot of Siri’s most advanced AI capabilities are presently powered by Google’s Gemini models.

In a recent development, at the same 2024 event where Google expressed doubts, Apple reiterated its commitment to its 2030 target. Then-CEO Tim Cook repeated this assurance later the same year, although admitted it would be challenging.

It has been revealed that more challenges, yes. But are we coming off the goal? No, definitely not. With more data centers, you use more renewable energy, and we’ve built that muscle now […] I feel very good about 2030.

In the company’s most recent environmental progress report, it said that it was was still using 100% renewable energy despite using over 2.5 billion kWh of electricity to power its data centers.

Sources indicate that we’re proud that 100 percent of that electricity came from renewable sources including solar, wind, and low-impact hydropower. To cover our needs, we build our own renewable power projects and work with utilities to purchase clean energy from locally obtained resources. We’re staying at 100 percent even as Apple’s data center capacity continues to grow.

The same report said the manufacturer had achieved zero water use for cooling at its latest data centers.

At our three newest data centers, we use high-efficiency air-cooled chillers instead of water-cooled systems, resulting in zero water use for cooling.

Recent findings suggest that however, the greatest challenge for Apple lies ahead. The reason that Google and Meta are now backtracking on their promises is that both companies now have massive AI capabilities. As yet, Apple does not.

Industry observers note that what happens as Apple expands Siri AI capabilities as usage increases, and as the firm moves into agentic AI features? Is it realistic for the company to maintain its 100% track record with vastly greater data center energy usage?

Greenpeace expressed its own doubts earlier this year.

“AI will be the defining test of Apple’s climate commitments,” spokesperson Avex Li indicates. “To preserve Tim Cook’s environmental legacy, the company will need to show that AI growth can be accommodated within its existing climate commitments through absolute emissions reductions, additional renewable energy investment, and longer-lasting products.”.

Apple did not respond directly but merely pointed to its past statements and most recent environmental progress report.

I don’t doubt the company’s desire to maintain its track record, but if Apple does join the likes of Google and Meta in becoming a major AI player, sticking to its 2030 timing is going to become increasingly difficult.

Raul Jimenez’s late penalty seals share of spoils for Wolves against Blackburn

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An injury-time penalty from returning hero Raul Jimenez ensured Wolves came away with a point in their Championship opener after Blackburn had produced a comeback.
  • Wolves led through Marshall Munetsi’s cool finish on 18 minutes only for Sean McLoughlin’s first Blackburn goal to draw the visitors level on 27 minutes with a well-timed run and header.
  • Recent findings suggest that the visitors turned the game around on 48 minutes through Andri Gudjohnsen’s close-range strike only for substitute Jimenez to level the game three minutes into injury time from the spot after Ryan Alebiosu handled the ball in the box.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An injury-time penalty from returning hero Raul Jimenez ensured Wolves came away with a point in their Championship opener after Blackburn had produced a comeback.

Wolves led through Marshall Munetsi’s cool finish on 18 minutes only for Sean McLoughlin’s first Blackburn goal to draw the visitors level on 27 minutes with a well-timed run and header.

Recent findings suggest that the visitors turned the game around on 48 minutes through Andri Gudjohnsen’s close-range strike only for substitute Jimenez to level the game three minutes into injury time from the spot after Ryan Alebiosu handled the ball in the box. Jimenez and his wife marked his return to Molineux by giving 5,000 fans black scarves emblazoned with the words ‘Si Senor’ - a nod to his song - and Jimenez did not disappoint as he rifled in his penalty.

LATE DRAMA! 😱Raul Jimenez cooly converts from the penalty spot, deep into added time to save a point for Wolves 🔥 pic.twitter.com/5h2lMxcHNU.

Industry observers note that cesar Peixoto wants Wolves to play with their heads rather than their hearts after the home side rescued a late point in the first game of the Championship season following relegation. Wolves replaced Rob Edwards with Portuguese coach Peixoto during the summer and he felt his side’s loss of organisation allowed Blackburn to take control of the game.

Recent findings suggest that peixoto remarked: “One point is not what we want, we want three points. We lost some organisation in the second half and played more with our hearts and not our heads and brains.

“We have to keep our mental stability during the 90 minutes because we’re better when we’re organised. We need to play our way with our identity. It’s a lesson for us to understand when we lose organisation it’s more difficult for us and more easy for the opposition.

According to recent reports, “We’re working hard to bring more solutions [into the club] but we need to work hard with the players we have. It’s the first game, there’s a lot to work on and a lot to improve.”.

Tony Mowbray took charge of Blackburn in the league for the first time since returning to the club for a second stint in the dugout. Rovers recorded their lowest league finish since Mowbray’s first stint in charge of the club last term but the Blackburn boss is confident his side have enough to beat the drop and climb up the table this campaign.

Recent findings suggest that mowbray stated: “Ultimately, it feels like a defeat, it’s a bit disappointing and a bit frustrating. I just felt a lot of decisions were starting to swing their way. It’s harsh to take, I don’t think they deserved a second goal. We asked the players to be brave and we were collectively very strong.

Recent findings suggest that “Everybody has us relegated, probably on the back of finishing 20th last season and losing a couple of our better players and not spending much money, which is a good motivation for the team. We deserved to win the game, we highlighted there’s enough quality to give teams problems and I hope there’s help on the way [in the transfer window].”.

The first chance of the season came the way of Blackburn as a cross-field pass found Alebiosu down the right, who floated a ball into the box only for an unmarked Oladipo Afolayan to head wide from eight-yards out.

However, Wolves scored the first goal of the new campaign when Fer Lopez played a defence-splitting through ball into the path of Munetsi, who coolly found the net with a first time effort from the edge of the penalty area.

"A vibrant Molineux rejoices!" 🎉Marshall Munetsi cooly slots home for Wolves to give them the lead on the opening night of the Championship season 🥶 pic.twitter.com/tVHdbNv3Hq.

Blackburn drew level through an unlikely source just nine minutes later as McLoughlin headed in his first-ever goal in English football in more than 150 games when he met Ryoya Morishita’s cross from the right at the near post.

The home side had chances to retake the lead before the break as Lopez curled a shot narrowly over the top from 20-yards while Kieran Trippier teed up Mateus Mane for a chance as the teenager found the top of the net from distance.

Blackburn turned the game on its head minutes after the break as Gudjohnsen turned home Afolayan’s deflected ball in from the right from close range to stun Molineux into silence.

"It's brilliantly worked by Blackburn Rovers!" 💥Andri Guðjohnsen finishes from close range to turn the game around and the visitors the lead 👏 pic.twitter.com/vkKQQezicK.

Peixoto introduced Jimenez from the bench on the hour mark but even the Mexican could not lift Wolves with Blackburn comfortable for long periods as frustration grew in the stands.

However, Alebiosu handled Jackson Tchatchoua’s cross from the left in injury time and the referee awarded a spot kick which allowed Jimenez to mark his Wolves return with an equaliser from 12-yards as he sent Balazs Toth the wrong way.

“I think it is a really harsh one. He [the referee] has to be sure at such a critical time of the game. And I do not think he can be sure. I think he has almost had a guess that he is in the box. It is such a major call.”.

“We see the ref’s position. The fact the ref makes the decision to give the penalty in my opinion, it is a bigger decision to give it then to not. We have got the luxury of the replays and we are still not sure. His whole body is outside the box.”.

“It looks outside the box to me [the penalty incident]. The still picture suggests to me it was outside the box. We can get better and we will have to. We have to be more dominant with the ball at times and be better in attack. We have done a lot of work on that in pre-season. Having been in this league a long time, the power of the dressing room is crucial and any motivation tool you can you use is vital. I think we will be fine. You have to enjoy football and love it. I think the boys enjoyed it tonight.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Obviously frustrated. The boys did everything to get the three points but it is gutting in the end. I thought I was outside the box when the ball came in and the decision went against us. They are saying it is in the box and it is frustrating. We dug deep and thought we had it. I cannot fault everyone as we all put in a shift, it was just the final details with the penalty decision. We deserved the three points. If we play like that every week, we will go far in the table.”.

When Wolverhampton Wanderers last attacked the Championship under a Portuguese manager new to English football, it proved a vintage season.

Molineux was under the spell of Nuno Espírito Santo in that 2017-18 campaign, and the substantial question is whether César Peixoto can lead a repeat nearly a decade later.

Peixoto was a surprise appointment in June, replacing Rob Edwards, and he has been entrusted with the mission of returning Wolves to the Premier League at the first time of asking.

“I have changed some things with set-pieces and some things in other moments of the game because I want the team to be organised and understand all the different moments within a match. During pre-season we have scored some goals from high pressing, but we will not be able to press high in every moment of every game. The players have to understand the game and recognise what each moment requires. It is key that we work as a team. When we can press high, we’ll press high. When we need to defend in a mid-block, we will stay organised. When the opposition pushes us deeper, which will sometimes happen, we have to be organised there as well.

“There are a lot of crosses in the Championship, for example, so the team needs to understand what to do in those situations. We want to play our football, be offensive and react strongly when we lose the ball, but we also need to understand the different moments of the game. I think we are at a good level to attack the Championship.”.
